title: Breath, the self's shadow
hookLine: breath just won the argument; now the third student asks where breath itself comes from, and the answer is a shadow
carry: breath is the shadow; the atman casts it
tomorrow: when you sleep, what in you stays awake?
last: PRANA: THE POWER ALL THE OTHERS RIDE ON.

cards: Breath has just been crowned. So the next student, Kausalya, son of Ashvala, does what a good student does after a big answer: he asks the question underneath it. Where is breath born from?
How does it come into this body, divide itself, and settle? How does it leave? Pippalada's reply begins with a raised eyebrow.
You're asking questions beyond questions, he says. But you are devoted to Brahman, so I'll answer. And the answer starts with something you can see on any sunny sidewalk.

teach.h: BREATH IS BORN FROM THE SELF.
teach.b: Pippalada says: breath is born from the self.

teach.h: AS A SHADOW FROM A PERSON.
teach.b: As a shadow falls from a person, so breath is cast from the self. And it comes into this body by the working of the mind. Sit with that picture.
A shadow is real. It moves, it has a shape, it can cover a whole wall. But it has no life of its own.
Take the person away and the shadow goes too. So breath, the king of yesterday's story, turns out to be the self's shadow: close, faithful, completely dependent.

teach.h: LIKE A KING WITH OFFICERS: FIVE BREATHS.
teach.b: Then the text describes how breath runs the body, like a king telling his officers: you govern these villages, you govern those. The main breath, prana, stays in the eyes and ears, the mouth and nose.
Apana, the down-going breath, works in the lower body. Samana, in the middle, carries the food offered into the body evenly, and from it, the text says, rise seven flames.
Vyana moves through the channels that branch out from the heart.

And udana, the up-going breath, rises through one channel at the end of life and carries a person on: to a good world for good deeds, a painful one for wrongs, and back to the human world for a mix of both.
Outside the body, the rising sun is breath too, and the power in the earth steadies the down-going breath. So, back to Kausalya's question beyond questions: where does breath come from?
From the atman, the self, the way a shadow comes from a person. That's the teaching. Breath is life, but breath isn't you.
The self casts it, and Hindus hold that the self doesn't end when the breath does.

how: Yoga and Ayurveda teachers still use the names of the five breaths, prana, apana, samana, vyana and udana, from texts like this one, to describe how breath works in the body.

o: a shadow, the way breath falls from the self
a sunny path that leads to the gods
the down-going breath in the lower body

games.q: the five breaths — tap the pairs.
p: rises and carries a person on

s: Pippalada says breath is born from food
he says breath is born from the self, as a shadow falls from a person.
but because the student is devoted to Brahman, he answers.
the text compares breath to a king with officers
the main breath assigns the others their places in the body.

games.q: breath holds up the whole body. you're Kausalya. what's the next question worth asking?
o: where is breath itself born from?
games.why: Pippalada calls it a question beyond questions and answers: breath is born from the self, as a shadow from a person.

practice: Watch the breath move the way you'd watch your shadow walk beside you, going where you go, changing shape. Then gently turn toward what the shadow falls from: the stillness that's aware of breathing.
You don't have to find it; just face that way, and let the breath keep moving on its own, close and faithful.

wordCard.voice: Chaya, a shadow. As a shadow falls from a person, so breath is cast from the self, Pippalada says, and it enters the body by the working of the mind.

orig.note: Sanskrit chāyā, shadow: 'as a shadow from a person, so breath from the self', Prashna 3.3.

carryVoice: Your line: breath is the shadow; the atman casts it. Tomorrow, a student follows the self into sleep. See you then.
